title: Cursor Lifecycle, Handlers and Set-Based Alternatives
description: Declare and close MySQL cursors correctly, handle end-of-data without stale processing, and compare bounded procedural calculations with equivalent set-based aggregates.

questions.question_text: What does a cursor provide inside a supported stored program?
options: An independently committed transaction per row
questions.explanation: Cursor iteration is a procedural access mechanism.

questions.question_text: Which declaration order is appropriate here?
options: Variables and conditions, then cursors, then handlers
questions.explanation: MySQL compound-block declaration rules matter.

questions.question_text: What does OPEN do?
questions.explanation: Opening begins cursor use under the engine contract.

questions.question_text: What does FETCH target count need to match?
questions.explanation: Each selected value needs a compatible destination.

questions.question_text: When should the loop check the done flag after FETCH?
options: Before processing the attempted fetched row
questions.explanation: The exhausted fetch must not cause stale-value processing.

questions.question_text: What input most directly challenges first-fetch exhaustion?
questions.explanation: The loop must terminate without processing any row.

questions.question_text: Can another no-row SELECT INTO trigger a block’s NOT FOUND handler?
options: No, the handler sees only cursor FETCH
Yes, depending on its scope and condition
questions.explanation: Handler scope must distinguish unrelated no-row operations.

questions.question_text: Why reset a reused done flag deliberately?
options: An earlier exhausted pass can leave it true
questions.explanation: State from one cursor lifetime must not silently end another.

questions.question_text: What does read-only describe for this cursor?
options: No other routine statement can ever write
questions.explanation: Separate writes still need their own design and restrictions.

questions.question_text: What does nonscrollable imply?
options: Forward fetch flow rather than arbitrary backward positioning
questions.explanation: Cursor capabilities differ from a general random-access collection.

questions.question_text: Does asensitive prove a fixed separately materialized snapshot in every execution?
questions.explanation: Visibility and buffering require the actual engine contract.

questions.question_text: With cap 50, what do 20, 80 and 0 contribute?
questions.explanation: The cap is applied to each eligible known amount.

questions.question_text: What is the resulting total for that three-row cap example?
questions.explanation: Twenty plus fifty plus zero equals seventy.

questions.question_text: Why explicitly exclude NULL amounts in the stated loop?
options: The contract does not treat missing amounts as known contributions
questions.explanation: Eligibility and accumulator missingness must be deliberate.

questions.question_text: Does CLOSE commit pending writes?
options: Only if the loop is empty
questions.explanation: Cursor cleanup and transaction completion are different operations.

questions.question_text: What set-based alternative expresses the count exercise?
options: COUNT over the same approved predicate
questions.explanation: Compare equivalent populations before measuring.

questions.question_text: What set-based alternative expresses the capped sum?
options: SUM ofLEAST over the same eligible population, with an explicit empty fallback
questions.explanation: The same row-level contribution rule must be preserved.

questions.question_text: Is DELIMITER a server SQL statement?
options: No, it is a directive in supporting clients
questions.explanation: Creation packaging depends on the client.

questions.question_text: Why can a very long cursor loop be operationally costly?
options: It can retain transaction resources and add procedural work
questions.explanation: Duration and actual operations determine resource costs.

questions.question_text: What does a successful one-session total not establish?
options: Provider compatibility, concurrent behavior or authorization
That the arithmetic matched that fixture
questions.explanation: Evidence boundaries remain separate.

Initialize zero and sum LEAST(amount, p_cap), checking the end flag before processing. Close the cursor and call with cap fifty. Return @capped_total AS capped_total.

edge_cases: An amount above the cap contributes the cap.
hints: Filter eligibility in the cursor query.

notes:
## Iterate only when row-by-row work is the intended tool

A stored-program cursor provides a controlled way to fetch rows from a query result one at a time inside supported procedural code. In MySQL, the documented cursor model is asensitive, read-only and nonscrollable. It is not an ordinary result set handed directly to a browser, and it is not automatically the best way to express a relational calculation. Use it when the procedural requirement justifies sequential handling, then compare a set-based alternative.

Imagine an equipment grant review where each approved request contributes up to a fixed per-request allowance. A cursor can fetch each eligible amount and accumulate its capped contribution. The same mathematical result can often be expressed more simply with SUM and LEAST. The exercise teaches cursor control and cleanup, not a claim that loops outperform aggregates or that a cursor is required for every multirow task.

## Declare objects in the supported order

Inside a MySQL compound block, local variables and conditions are declared before cursors, and cursors before handlers. Declarations precede executable statements in their scope. A NOT FOUND handler can set a local done flag when FETCH reaches the end. Clear declaration order and small scopes make the control flow easier to verify and avoid turning a syntax lesson into a guess about which declaration the server accepts.

```sql
-- Body fragment inside a supported compound routine:
DECLARE done BOOL DEFAULT FALSE;
DECLARE v_amount INT;
DECLARE amount_cursor CURSOR FOR
  SELECT amount FROM cursor_requests
  WHERE status='approved' ORDER BY request_id;
DECLARE CONTINUE HANDLER FOR NOT FOUND SET done=TRUE;
```

The cursor query defines its eligible population and any meaningful iteration order. A WHERE status='approved' filter excludes cancelled requests before fetching. An ORDER BY request_id makes the sequence deliberate when the operation depends on order. It does not grant authorization or lock every relevant row automatically; transaction isolation and the complete routine's access contract still determine observation and concurrency behavior.

## Follow OPEN, FETCH and CLOSE explicitly

OPEN establishes the cursor's result-processing context. FETCH attempts to place the next row's selected values into compatible local variables. CLOSE ends the cursor's use and releases its associated cursor resources under the engine contract. Fetch target count and types must match the cursor query's selected values. A cursor that selects an amount and identity needs two appropriate targets rather than one variable reused ambiguously.

The standard loop fetches first, checks whether the end handler set done, and processes the fetched value only when a row was actually obtained. Checking done after the arithmetic can process a stale variable once more when the final FETCH finds no row. A zero-row input should therefore be an early test case, not an afterthought once the happy path works.

```sql
OPEN amount_cursor;
read_loop: LOOP
  FETCH amount_cursor INTO v_amount;
  IF done THEN LEAVE read_loop; END IF;
  SET p_total=p_total+LEAST(v_amount,p_cap);
END LOOP;
CLOSE amount_cursor;
```

This fragment assumes the total and cap were initialized and validated under the surrounding routine's contract. It does not define how NULL or negative amounts should contribute. The lesson's worked cap exercise includes only known nonnegative approved amounts in the cursor query. Missing or rejected values are excluded explicitly rather than relying on accidental NULL arithmetic to erase the accumulator.

## Treat NOT FOUND scope carefully

A NOT FOUND handler in a block can also be activated by another no-row operation in that scope, such as a suitable SELECT INTO. If an unrelated lookup sets the same done flag, the loop can stop early even though the cursor still has rows. Use nested blocks or otherwise deliberate handler scope when mixing cursor iteration with additional lookups. State which operation is intended to set the end-of-cursor flag.

Reset the done flag appropriately before a fresh iteration if the routine reopens a cursor under supported control flow. A variable left true from a prior exhausted cursor can make a later pass appear empty. Do not reuse one flag casually across several cursors with different lifetimes. Two-cursor algorithms need an explicit policy for which source's exhaustion ends which part of the computation.

## Keep arithmetic and NULL policy visible

For a cap of fifty, approved known amounts 20, 80 and 0 contribute 20, 50 and 0. The expected total is seventy. An approved NULL amount is excluded by the stated query, not treated as a secretly known zero. A cancelled eighty contributes nothing. These cases distinguish eligibility from per-row transformation and show how one accidental NULL addition could otherwise make the running total unknown.

For a pure count of approved requests, incrementing an integer counter per fetched row should equal the set-based COUNT over the same eligible query. A mismatch suggests duplicate processing, wrong handler scope, an omitted condition or a changed source observation. Keep the query and expected identity population beside the loop rather than debugging only the final numeric result.

## Understand the cursor's capabilities and limits

Read-only means the cursor itself does not provide an update-through-cursor interface for fetched rows. Nonscrollable means the supported fetch flow advances rather than offering arbitrary backward positioning. Asensitive does not promise a universally fixed materialized snapshot independent of implementation. Do not infer a particular locking, visibility or physical buffering behavior from the word cursor alone.

A separate UPDATE inside the loop is a new operation with its own authorization, locking and consistency implications. If the requirement changes the same population being scanned, inspect engine restrictions and the intended transaction semantics carefully. A cursor is not a substitute for a stable identity, an appropriate current-state check or a verified concurrency protocol. Keep purely read-only learning loops separate from production mutation designs.

## Coordinate error cleanup and transaction ownership

An exception can leave the routine's intended work incomplete. Define how cursor resources are closed and how the caller learns the failure. The transaction owner must decide whether supported pending writes are rolled back; closing a cursor is not COMMIT or ROLLBACK. A routine helper must not silently commit its caller's transaction merely because its loop finished successfully.

Keep long-running iteration bounded. A loop over millions of rows can hold transaction resources and prolong locks or snapshot retention depending on its operations. Include cancellation and failure paths in integration tests. Returning a pooled connection with unresolved work can affect another request, and a lost commit response still requires reconciliation if the routine performed a business effect.

## Compare a set-based formulation before choosing the loop

The capped total can be written as SUM(LEAST(amount, p_cap)) over the same known nonnegative approved population, with COALESCE supplying zero for no qualifying rows when that is the intended contract. COUNT can directly express the count exercise. These forms can reduce procedural overhead and make the data operation easier for the optimizer to plan, but actual performance still needs representative measurement.

Some tasks need ordered procedural state that is not captured by a simple aggregate. Even then, window functions, recursive queries or a carefully designed relational transformation can sometimes express the requirement more clearly. Compare correctness, maintainability and operational behavior as well as timing. Do not introduce a cursor solely because an application-language for-loop feels familiar.

## Build a reproducible stored-program lab

Creation of a compound procedure in a command-line client can require a temporary DELIMITER directive. That directive belongs to the client parser rather than server SQL. A driver that submits the complete CREATE statement can need a different packaging approach. Record the execution client and engine before presenting a script as directly portable to every judge.

Use synthetic rows with explicit identifiers and retain ordering in the final checker. A successful total alone is insufficient if two errors cancel numerically. Include a single row, empty input, only cancelled rows, only missing amounts and a cap boundary. Compare the cursor result with an independently reasoned set-based expression over the exact same eligible population.

## Solve two cursor exercises

First exercise: create a routine that counts approved request rows using a cursor, OPEN, FETCH, end handling and CLOSE. On the shared fixture’s four approved rows and one cancelled row, the count is four; the approved row with NULL amount still counts. Empty input and only-cancelled input return zero. The result should match COUNT over the same predicate without processing a stale final fetch variable.

Second exercise: accumulate LEAST(amount, cap) only for approved, known, nonnegative amounts. With cap fifty and values 20, 80, 0, NULL plus a cancelled 100, the result is seventy. Compare the loop with the set-based sum and explain each excluded row. Continue with [stored procedures](/learning/dbms-sql-tutorial/stored-procedure-contracts), [aggregate functions](/learning/dbms-sql-tutorial/aggregate-functions) and [window functions](/learning/dbms-sql-tutorial/window-functions-ranking-and-frames) to choose a suitable relational or procedural tool.

diagrams.caption: Fetch must succeed before the loop processes its variables
diagrams.description: An empty cursor immediately sets the end flag. A correct loop checks after FETCH before using its variables, then closes the cursor and lets the transaction owner resolve the outcome.
